(Day 9 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: what makes up an AI)

AI, AI, AI. As I said in the first post in this series, it feels like a decade has passed since October 2025, and that’s because of AI. For all the talk of AI, though, it seems like people don’t really understand it that well. That’s a problem if you’re responsible for any part of AI security. People talk about AI as one thing, a magic box of sorts, but it’s really a stack of parts. Those parts are data, a model, hardware, software that runs the model, and the applications and tools wrapped around it. Each part does a different job, and as such, each part has its own security concerns.

Most AI security concerns are familiar, though. They are about data, access, and software supply chains, which security teams have dealt with for decades. A few are new, though. This post takes AI apart one piece at a time: what each part does, and what to watch for from a security point of view. It assumes you know more about infrastructure than data science.

Where an AI Gets Its Intelligence

Training Data

A model learns from examples. For the large language models (LLMs) behind most AI tools, those examples are enormous amounts of text, and often code and images, too. The model doesn’t store that data the way a database does. It learns patterns from it, so what goes in shapes what comes out. There is an old term in computers, “Garbage In, Garbage Out,” that is applicable here. A data poisoning attack is where someone deliberately slips garbage into the training data to change how the model behaves. Sensitive data in a training set can resurface in the model’s answers. Someone can also bias its answers on purpose.

Training data raises intellectual property questions, too. Public models learn from huge amounts of text and code collected from the internet. Courts are still working out when the law allows that. A model can sometimes reproduce copyrighted text or licensed code from its training data nearly word for word. That becomes your problem if it ends up in your product. Open models come with their own licenses, and some limit commercial use or how you can use the model. Your own intellectual property is at stake as well. Some hosted AI services keep what you send them, or train on it.

If you train or adapt a model, AI security starts with the data. Know where it came from and who could have changed it. Check that you have the right to use it, and whether anyone is keeping your own data.

The AI Model

The model itself is a large file, or a set of files, full of numbers called weights. When you send a model text, it first turns that text into numbers. Those numbers flow through layers of simple math units. Each unit takes the numbers from the layer before it and multiplies each one by its own weight. Then it adds them up and passes the result on. A large weight means the number it multiplies matters a lot. A small one means that number barely matters, and a negative one pushes the result the other way. It’s the same idea as a weighted average, where some scores count more toward a final grade than others.

After the last layer, the numbers become a score for every possible next word, or piece of a word. Those scores come entirely from your text and the weights. Give a model “The capital of France is,” and the weights tip the scores toward “Paris.” Training adjusts the weights a tiny bit at a time. It keeps going until the scores reliably favor the right next word, or the right next step in a task. Models with billions of weights are common, and together those weights hold everything the model has learned.

An AI Model Is a Little Like a Brain

A model works a little like a human brain. Its designers loosely based the math units on neurons, and the weights on the connections between neurons. That’s why “neural network” is the name for models like these. A human brain can’t do much on its own. It needs external parts, like eyes and ears and hands and legs, to get things done. Same for a model. Unlike a human brain, though, a model has no persistent memory of your last conversation. It starts over every time. Text goes in and text comes out. Anything more, like looking something up, reading a file, or sending an email, comes from the software around the model. The tools and agents covered below handle that.

AI Model Files and Formats

Model files are valuable. Training a large model costs a great deal, so the weights are intellectual property worth stealing. Model files can also be a direct AI security risk. Model makers distribute models in several formats, such as GGUF, safetensors, ONNX, and pickle. Some of these formats, like pickle, can contain code or other instructions that run when the model loads. GGUF and safetensors hold weights and settings without code, which makes them safer, but not risk-free. The software that reads them can have bugs, too. In 2024, researchers found that one popular tool would run code hidden in a GGUF file’s chat template. That’s a setting that tells the model how to format a conversation.

Treat models as part of your software supply chain. Check where each one came from, and prefer safetensors or GGUF over pickle-based formats. Keep the software that loads them patched, and control who can copy them.

Fine-Tuning

Most organizations don’t train models at all. They use an existing model, often called a foundation model, as it comes. They customize its answers with prompts and with their own documents through retrieval, covered below. Some go a step further and fine-tune a model. That means training it a little more on a smaller set of their own examples.

People fine-tune to change how a model behaves more than what it knows. A fine-tuned model might learn a company’s writing style, the vocabulary of a specialized field, or how to fill out a particular form the same way every time. Fine-tuning can also teach a smaller, cheaper model to do one narrow job nearly as well as a much larger one.

The most common technique, called LoRA (low-rank adaptation), leaves the original weights alone. Instead, it trains a small set of extra weights. That often keeps the job small enough for one server instead of a data center. The training saves those extra weights as a separate file, often in safetensors or GGUF format. The name for that file is an “adapter,” or just “a LoRA.” The adapter is a fraction of the size of the original model. The software applies it on top of the original when the model loads. You can also merge it into the original to produce one new, complete model file.

Protecting Fine-Tuned Models

Fine-tuning bakes your examples into the weights. Someone can sometimes coax a fine-tuned model into repeating what it learned. That makes the model and its outputs as sensitive as the data behind them. The result is also intellectual property in its own right, built from your data and the work of preparing it. Adapters are small and easy to copy. Because the original model is often public, the adapter is the part that’s uniquely yours. Whatever you build still carries the original model’s license terms, too.

If you wouldn’t give someone the data, think carefully before giving them a model or adapter fine-tuned on it.

Running an AI Model

Hardware

Models run on accelerators, mostly graphics processing units (GPUs), because the work involves a huge number of simple calculations done in parallel. Large models need a lot of GPU memory. That’s why GPUs are often the costliest part of an AI environment, and the hardest to get time on. GPUs have their own drivers and firmware and software stacks that require upkeep and security updates, like everything else in the AI stack.

GPUs are too expensive to leave idle, so they’re often shared, and sharing calls for proper isolation. You can split some GPUs into instances, with hardware walls between them. Newer GPUs also use techniques similar to confidential computing on CPUs to protect data and models while they’re in use.

Patch GPU drivers and firmware with everything else. Decide which workloads can share a GPU and how much separation they need. Consider confidential computing for the most sensitive work.

The Inference Server

“Inference” is the name for running a trained model to get answers. An inference server is the software that loads the model onto the GPUs and answers requests, usually through an API on the network. Think of it as the application server of the AI stack. If the model were a Spring application, the inference server would be the Apache Tomcat it runs in. Tomcat loads the app, listens on the network, and handles every request. Same for the inference server. Most AI applications talk to a model this way. That makes an AI inference server a network service, with all the security needs of one. Some are easy to stand up with no authentication at all, which is a problem, of course. An exposed endpoint gives anyone free use of your expensive GPUs, and a direct way to attack the model. Answering each request also takes real GPU time, so a flood of requests can run up your costs or tie up your hardware.

Put authentication, isolation, patching, monitoring, and rate limits on every inference server before someone else finds it.

Prompts and the Context Window

A prompt is what you send the model, and it’s often text. However, there are layers to prompts, too. You might tell a model “please check my grammar,” but what the model receives is much more. A typical request to an AI assistant stacks up something like this:

  • System prompt. Instructions from whoever built the application, and sometimes from the model’s provider. They cover what the assistant is for, what tone to use, and what it should refuse.
  • Tool descriptions. If the application gives the model tools, it describes each one, so the model knows what it can ask for.
  • Saved context. Things the application remembers about you, like your preferences or earlier notes.
  • Retrieved documents and attachments. Passages pulled from a knowledge base, plus any files you attached.
  • The conversation so far. Every earlier message, from both you and the model.
  • Your message. “Please check my grammar,” plus the text you pasted in.

The application stitches all of that together and sends it as one long piece of text. It uses the chat template mentioned earlier to mark which part came from whom. The “context window” is the name for everything the model can see at once. Models read and write text in small pieces called tokens, roughly three-quarters of an English word each. Each model’s context window holds a limited number of them. When a conversation runs long, applications drop or summarize the oldest parts, and the model forgets the details.

Prompt Injection

The context window is where the most important security weakness unique to AI lives. Every layer arrives as one stream of tokens. As a result, a model can’t reliably tell instructions from data, or which layer a piece of text came from. If a document or web page in the context contains text like “ignore your previous instructions,” the model may follow it. That’s called prompt injection, and nobody has a complete fix for it. System prompts aren’t secret, either, because users can often get the model to reveal them.

Plan as if any text the model reads could try to give it orders, and keep secrets out of system prompts.

Guardrails

Guardrails are the checks that keep a model’s behavior within bounds, and they usually come in layers. Model makers build some into the model itself, training it to refuse certain requests. Some live in the system prompt, where the application tells the model what it should and shouldn’t do. That’s the easiest guardrail to add and the easiest to get around. It sits in the same stream of text as anything an attacker can write.

The rest are separate filters that check what goes into the model and what comes out. Some are simple rules, like a pattern that catches credit card numbers before they leave. Others are smaller AI models trained to spot harmful requests, prompt injection attempts, or answers that wander off topic. Because they sit outside the model, they’re harder to talk past than instructions in a prompt.

All of these help with AI security, but none of them is a security boundary. Attackers probe guardrails constantly, and a determined one can often find wording that gets through.

Use guardrails as one layer among several, alongside access controls, isolation, and human review.

Outputs

All of those things, and we finally get to the output! Here’s how it comes together. The application assembles the layered prompt, and the model turns it into tokens. Those tokens flow through the weights to produce a score for every possible next token. The model picks one and adds it to the end. Then it repeats the process, a word or so at a time, until it finishes the answer. Because models build answers one token at a time, people measure output speed in tokens per second. That’s also why answers often appear on screen a few words at a time. Guardrails may check the result on its way out.

The model generates the answer instead of looking it up. Each word is the model’s best prediction of what should come next, given everything in the context window and everything it learned in training. That’s why answers read smoothly even when they’re wrong, and why models sometimes hallucinate: they state wrong things with complete confidence. It’s also why someone can steer the output. Anyone who can get text into the context window can shift those predictions. Some applications run what a model writes as code, a database query, or a command. There, an attacker who influences the model influences those, too, turning a quirk of AI into a security hole.

Treat model output as untrusted input, and check it the way you would check anything a user typed. Keep a person involved in decisions that matter.

Giving an AI Your Data and Tools

Retrieval and Vector Databases

A model only knows what it learned in training and what is in its context window. To answer questions about your own documents, many applications use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The application searches your documents for passages related to the question, adds them to the prompt, and the model answers using them.

That search usually runs on embeddings, which are lists of numbers that represent the meaning of a piece of text. A vector database stores the embeddings and quickly finds text with similar meaning. The vector database holds your documents, or something close to them. Researchers have shown that they can sometimes turn embeddings back into a close approximation of the original text.

The bigger AI security issue is permissions. If the retrieval step ignores who is asking, the AI will cheerfully hand a user passages from documents they never had permission to open. Retrieved documents are also a common path for prompt injection. Anyone who can edit a document the system reads can hide instructions in it.

If you use RAG, protect the vector database like the source data. Make sure your access controls carry through into retrieval, and control who can add documents to the sources it reads.

Tools, Agents, and Harnesses

On its own, that brain only produces text. Give it tools, and it can act. Tools are functions the model can ask for, such as searching the web, reading a file, sending an email, or calling another system’s API. The model never runs a tool itself. It writes a request, in a format described in its prompt, and the software around it does the work.

The “harness” is the name for that software. The harness builds the layered prompt, sends it to the model, and reads the answer. Then it runs any tools the model asked for and feeds the results back in for the next round. An AI agent is a model and a harness working through that loop over and over. Together, they plan and carry out a series of steps with less human involvement along the way. The harness decides what the model can touch, which makes it one of the most important pieces of AI security.

MCP Servers and Tool Risk

Many tools now connect through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a widely used standard. An MCP server is a small program that offers a set of tools to any harness that speaks MCP. Those tools might reach a ticketing system, a database, or a file share. Some run on the same machine as the harness, and others run across the network. Either way, an MCP server usually holds the credentials it needs to reach those systems. It’s also software someone else probably wrote, so it belongs in your inventory and your supply chain reviews.

Tools raise the stakes. Prompt injection without tools produces a bad answer. Prompt injection with tools can produce a bad action. An agent acts with whatever permissions its tools have. That makes it a lot like a service account that takes orders from whatever text it reads. MCP servers add a risk of their own. A malicious or compromised one can hide instructions in its tool descriptions, which land in the prompt with everything else.

If you give a model tools, give them the least privilege they need, and use only MCP servers you’ve reviewed. Require a person to approve consequential actions, like deleting data or sending money. Have the harness log what agents do, so you can tell afterward what happened and why.

Putting the AI Parts Together

Where an AI system’s parts run largely influences who has to secure them, how they do it, and how much trust you need. When you use a hosted AI service, the provider runs the model, the hardware, and the inference server. Your prompts, documents, and data leave your environment to get there. After that, you have little visibility beyond what the contract says. You can’t easily see who can access your data, how long the provider keeps it, or whether it trains future models on it. The provider usually shares the infrastructure with its other customers. It can also change the model or its terms on its own schedule. And a breach or outage on its side becomes your problem, too. Hosted AI is convenient, but every part you don’t run is a part you can’t secure, audit, or recover yourself.

Running AI Yourself

When you run AI yourself, all the parts live in your environment. That might be on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), perhaps with tools like VMware vDefend. Your data stays with you, protected and secured along with your other workloads. You decide who can reach it, how long you keep it, and when a model changes. VMware Private AI Services, which is a native part of VCF, helps immensely with model provenance, access control, and deployment workflow. VCF Operations helps you monitor and plan capacity. Snapshots, replication, and VMware Live Recovery de-risk security patching and updating AI workloads, just as they do with all other applications.

In the end, AI is a very useful tool, and a force multiplier for organizations, but it isn’t magic. It is data, files, software, and hardware. Once you know what each one does, you can see where the attack surfaces are so you can protect them.

item.content:encoded:
As a TAM, I’ve noticed a recurring theme in almost every customer conversation lately: the critical need to balance rigorous information security with operational simplification. While teams still demand robust, enterprise-grade capabilities (especially to defend their infrastructure), they’re looking for ways to cut through the noise – removing the friction from how they adopt, manage, secure, and scale their solutions.

That’s exactly what inspired VMware Cloud Foundation’s most recent release, which is particularly relevant as part of our Cybersecurity Month Blog series. In my previous blogs, I’ve covered how VCF 9 is modernizing the private cloud and simplifying Day 2 operations. Today, let’s look at the practical aspects of upgrading to VCF 9.1.1.

Let’s walk through the newest, highly requested “quality of life” improvements and architectural capabilities designed specifically to accelerate your adoption journey, reduce your footprint, and make upgrading to a hardened, protected environment easier than ever.

Phase 1: Plan with Confidence – The Upgrade Prep

The first step to a successful upgrade is removing the guesswork and the historical roadblocks. VCF 9.1.1 delivers massive wins on both fronts.

Consult the VCF Upgrade Planning Tool

Before you touch a single binary or schedule a maintenance window, your very first stop should be the VCF Upgrade Planner. We first published this tool earlier this year when we released 9.1 to help customers better understand their own, customized path forward into VCF 9.1.

If you aren’t using this tool yet, you are missing out on one of the most powerful pre-flight checks available. The VCF Upgrade Planner, now upgraded for VCF 9.1.1, takes the complexity out of lifecycle management by allowing you to map your exact current state to your desired VCF 9.1.1 end state. It identifies specific upgrade prerequisites based on your exact configuration, highlights any potential interoperability considerations, and provides a customized, step-by-step roadmap for your environment. Below is an example of the information necessary to customize your upgrade plan within the tool.

The tool clearly outlines where safe stopping points are during the process so you can spread the process over multiple change windows if necessary. You can even export the entire upgrade plan in various formats to easily include in your internal change management tools such as Jira or ServiceNow. The screenshot below shows the process output for an example environment.

You no longer need to guess your steps or consult multiple documentation sources to ensure a successful upgrade – the VCF Upgrade Planner plans and documents it comprehensively.

Celebrate: The “Back-in-Time” Upgrade Restriction is Lifted 

While back-in-time upgrade restrictions are a reality of parallel release cycles and patch management, I am thrilled to share that VCF 9.1.1 specifically clears the most recent hurdles blocking your upgrade path.

For context, a back-in-time scenario occurs when you apply a critical security patch to your environment, and that patched product version contains newer code than the target major release code. Earlier this year, administrators had to make a tough choice: apply the critical security fixes in vSphere 8.0 Update 3k or VCF 5.2.4 to patch vulnerabilities but temporarily lose the ability to upgrade directly to VCF 9.1.0 or keep your VCF 9.1 upgrade path open but leave critical vulnerabilities unpatched.

With the release of VCF 9.1.1, that restriction is officially resolved. If you are currently running vSphere 8.0U3j, vSphere 8.0U3k, VCF 9.0.2 EP2, or VCF 5.2.4, your forward upgrade path is restored. You no longer have to choose between keeping your environment secure with the latest asynchronous patches and advancing to the newest VCF architecture. 

However, a word to the wise: the nature of software lifecycles means this open window is not guaranteed to last. While your path to 9.1.1 is clear today, a future zero-day vulnerability could force you to apply a new out-of-band patch to your current environment, potentially introducing a brand-new back-in-time restriction. You can always check the validity of your upgrade path using the Product Interoperability Matrix.

The takeaway here is simple: strike while the iron is hot. If you have been sitting in a holding pattern waiting for the green light to upgrade, this is it. Capitalize on this cleared path and make your move to 9.1.1 before the next unpredictable security advisory changes the equation again.

Phase 2: Test and Validate – The Sandbox Experience

You want to get your hands on the new code, test your automation, and train your team – but you shouldn’t have to rack a mountain of servers just to build a sandbox. 9.1.1 gives you two brilliant ways to kick the tires.

Spin Up a Single ESXi Host Deployment (Directly from the UI)

Building a proof-of-concept (PoC) or a lab environment used to be a hardware-heavy endeavor that required strict minimums. With VCF 9.1.1, we have introduced official support for a Single ESX Host Deployment directly within the VCF Installer UI. Previously, deploying VCF on a single node for lab purposes required specialized API calls, JSON manipulation, and your comfort with going outside a documented process. Now, it is a native, click-through option in the Installer.

This is absolutely perfect for administrators and architects who want to validate API scripts, test integrations, or simply familiarize themselves with the 9.1.1 interface with the absolute minimal hardware investment. Keep in mind that while the VCF Installer UI does allow for single node deployments, production deployments must still adhere to the published host minimums to remain supported.

Explore the New Hands-on Labs 

What if you want to test drive VCF 9.1.1 but have zero hardware available? We’ve got you covered.

Freshly updated and showcased for the first time at VMware Explore 2026, the new catalog of VCF 9.1 Hands-on Labs (HOLs) are now live and available globally. These labs are the fastest, most risk-free way to experience the new capabilities immediately. Whether you want to test the new lifecycle management workflows, explore the updated UI, or walk through a simulated deployment, the HOLs provide a pristine, pre-configured environment right in your browser. Send the link to your entire operations team – it’s the best free training available.

Phase 3: Deploy with Unprecedented Flexibility – The Architectural Wins

Once you are ready to architect your 9.1.1 environment, you’ll find that we’ve made some serious optimizations to how VCF consumes resources, allowing you to do much more with less.

Reclaim Resources with a Reduced Management Services Footprint

Introduced in VCF 9.1, the VCF Management Services consolidated previously fragmented administrative appliances into a modern, unified, containerized control plane. In VCF 9.1.1, our engineering teams have heavily optimized that architecture, resulting in a significantly reduced VCF Management Services footprint. You can see the specific decrease in the chart below, but we’re talking about a ~40% reduction for each deployment type when compared to 9.1!

By streamlining the backend services and reducing overhead, we are giving those resources back to you. This means you can reclaim valuable CPU and Memory and reallocate it to your actual revenue-generating tenant workloads, driving a much better Return on Investment for your existing private cloud hardware.

Already deployed a 9.1 environment with the original sizing? Use the script provided in our Knowledge Base article to adjust your existing deployment to the new, smaller footprint.

Deploy Anywhere with the New “Small HA” Option 

For many customers High Availability (HA) is a non-negotiable requirement for modern businesses, but previously choosing a HA architecture required moving to a medium size deployment with a significant (over double) CPU/Memory requirement. Enter the Small HA deployment option. This brand-new profile bridges the gap for customers who need enterprise-grade resilience but operate in constrained environments. This new deployment option reduces the resource requirements for the minimal HA deployment by nearly 50%. The chart below highlights in red the resource requirements for the smallest supported HA deployment in 9.1 compared to 9.1.1.

The time to act is now

The journey to modernizing your private cloud doesn’t have to be a grind. VCF 9.1.1 was built directly around your feedback – removing historical upgrade blockers, shrinking the management footprint, and providing simple and lightweight ways to test and deploy.

Beyond the architectural wins, there is a calendar reality we all need to prepare for: vSphere 8.0 and the VCF 5.x stack reach the End of General Support (EOGS) on October 11, 2027. If you were planning to simply step up to the initial VCF 9.0 release to buy more time, be aware of the new VCF support model and release cadence. End of General Support for 9.0 occurs on September 17, 2027. Let that sink in: landing on 9.0 doesn’t extend your runway past the October 2027 deadline; it actually arrives a few weeks earlier.

This is why aiming directly for VCF 9.1.1 is so critical. Getting to 9.1.1 not only unlocks the footprint reductions and HA options we’ve discussed, but it fundamentally resets your support runway, extending your general support lifecycle to August 2028.

Don’t delay – start your checklist today. Open up the VCF Upgrade Planner, map out your environment, and see just how fast you can accelerate your adoption of VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1.

item.content:encoded:
(Day 8 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: patching)

There is a saying that “slow is smooth, and smooth is fast.” It’s usually credited to the military. It means that rushing leads to mistakes, and cleaning up after them takes longer than doing the work carefully in the first place. Thinking about it more, we realized this idea applies to patching, too.

The number of vulnerabilities has grown enormously, and much of that is due to AI and its ability to find vulnerabilities quickly. Put frankly, nobody can patch fast enough to stay ahead of all of it. Or, stated a different way, nobody wants to. It takes constant heroic effort, and teams that try burn out. The answer, then, is not to patch faster. It is to make patching so routine that it barely needs anyone’s attention. Who cares how fast patching is if you don’t have to do much to make it happen?

This post is a collection of ideas for getting there, collected from presentations and discussions over the last few years.

No More Picking and Choosing

Patching has to happen, and you need to take all the patches. That has actually always been true, but for years, organizations could get away with skipping updates, waiting a few quarters, or applying only the ones that looked scary. Attackers were not nearly as relentless as they are now.

That doesn’t work anymore. As we covered in our post about vulnerabilities, attackers chain small flaws together, and AI has made building those chains fast and cheap. A backlog of Low and Moderate issues is just as helpful to a modern attacker as a single critical issue.

Triaging vulnerabilities has also become much harder. A CVSS score can no longer tell you how useful a flaw will be to an attacker, and even experts struggle to judge that. You can’t always tell what an update fixes, either. Every detail a vendor publishes teaches attackers where to look, so release notes may not show how important an update really is. Picking and choosing patches by severity no longer works. Take them all.

At the same time, nobody can patch everything the moment it ships. That’s where defense-in-depth and the rest of your security design come in. Isolating management interfaces, controlling who has access, and hardening your systems all buy you time. That time lets patching happen on a steady schedule instead of in a panic.

Build Systems That Are Easy to Patch

A lot of what makes patching hard comes from how clusters were built, as well as organizational policies that let applications dictate how infrastructure has to behave. The current AI worries make this a good time to renegotiate some of that.

Trust vMotion

VMware vSphere vMotion is mature and reliable. For all but a small number of applications, it moves running workloads between hosts without anyone noticing. It is the foundation that lets you patch a host in a way that’s invisible to workloads and their downstream consumers.

Some workloads genuinely can’t be moved, such as some VMs that use passthrough hardware devices, or ones with real-time requirements (telco applications, etc.). Others have owners who insist they can’t be moved. Test that claim. Applications that cannot live-migrate present a serious issue to infrastructure security, and many applications that people think can’t move turn out to move just fine. Try vMotion on them in a controlled way, outside business hours, with the application owner involved. In many cases, organizations have found that the major improvements to vMotion in the vSphere 7 timeframe let the application move without disruption.

For the applications that truly can’t move, many organizations put them on their own cluster and patch it on its own schedule, with planned downtime. The rest of the environment can then stay current without waiting on them. That cluster will likely be patched less often, so treat it as higher risk. Give it tighter network isolation and stricter access controls than the rest of the environment.

Also keep in mind that VMware Tools has pre-vMotion hooks you can use to automate things, like a drain-stop of a cluster node in a load-balanced environment. Similarly, VMware vSphere Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.0 and later works to minimize the number of vMotions while patching, so any actual disruption to an application would likely be only once.

Keep Spare Capacity for Patching

Design every cluster with at least N+1 capacity, meaning enough spare resources to run every workload with one host out of service. That leaves room to take a host out for patching. Then protect that space for the infrastructure. A cluster that’s 100% full is at N capacity. The +1 is yours.

If it helps to have a technical limit to point to, let VMware vSphere High Availability (HA) admission control enforce it for you. When someone wants to power on more VMs than the cluster can protect, admission control says no, and you don’t have to.

Respect the vSAN Timers

When a host enters maintenance mode, VMware vSAN asks what to do with the data on it. For routine patching, use the default, “Ensure accessibility.” It moves only the data needed to keep every VM’s storage accessible, and then vSAN waits before it starts rebuilding anything. That wait is the object repair timer, which is 60 minutes by default. If each host finishes patching and rejoins within that window, vSAN does not need to rebuild data.

Don’t override this with “Full data migration” for routine patching. Evacuating every host’s data, one host at a time, turns a quick reboot into hours of data movement across the cluster. It adds load and risk to every patch cycle for very little benefit. It also wears out your storage faster. Flash devices, whether SSD or NVMe, are consumable components that can handle only a finite amount of writing over their lifetime. Copying a host’s worth of data around the cluster every patch cycle uses up a substantial amount of it. Save full migration for hosts that will be out of service for days, or that are being retired.

Keep the Image Lean

VMware vSphere Lifecycle Manager (vLCM) manages each cluster with a single image. The image holds a base VMware ESX version, your server vendor’s add-on, drivers and firmware, and any extra components. Keep that image lean. Hardware vendor ISOs often include custom drivers and applications for a wide range of hardware and uses, and you may not need all of them. Build the image to include only the drivers your hardware uses and the components your environment actually runs, and nothing else. Every extra component needs testing and has to stay compatible, and problems with extras like these are a common reason an upgrade stops partway through.

Update Firmware and Drivers Together

Server vendors generally test new firmware with new drivers. Running a current ESX build with firmware from years ago, or the reverse, puts you in a combination that nobody has tested. Updating both together leads to fewer surprises. Your server vendor and the Broadcom Compatibility Guide list which combinations of firmware, drivers, and ESX are supported.

vLCM can include firmware in the cluster image when your server vendor provides a hardware support manager, so firmware and drivers move together. A hardware support manager is an extra component you may not want to run, secure, back up, and audit, though. Another idea is that many servers’ out-of-band management controllers can stage a firmware update so it applies at the next reboot. The host then picks up the firmware during the same restart as the ESX patch.

If you stage firmware that way, turn off Quick Boot on those hosts. Quick Boot speeds up restarts by skipping the server’s Power On Self-Test (POST) initialization, so a staged firmware update may not apply.

It can also help to set one host to download and stage new firmware automatically. That gives you a place to see whether new firmware fixes a problem, or causes one, before the rest of the cluster gets it.

Roll Out Patches in Stages

Patch VMware vCenter first, then one host, and then wait a few hours before doing the rest. If a problem would only show up during a daily peak or a nightly batch job, wait until the host has run through that, too. Test environments are important, but a test environment is never quite like production, so treat that first production host as the real test. Watch that host closely, but don’t let nerves turn into not patching.

Some organizations also wait a few days after a release to see whether others report problems. For routine updates, that can be reasonable. For a vulnerability that is being actively exploited, waiting is usually riskier than patching. The VMware Security Advisory (VMSA) and its companion Q&A, when there is one, can help you decide.

DRS rules can help with these processes:

  • Put low-priority VMs on the first host. Use VM-host rules to place some lower-priority VMs on the host you usually patch first. Test, development, and other Tier 3 workloads are good candidates. If something goes wrong, it affects workloads that matter less. Make them “should” rules, not “must” rules, so DRS can still move those VMs when the host enters maintenance mode.
  • Keep redundant VMs on separate hosts. Use anti-affinity rules for VMs that provide the same service. Examples include a pair of domain controllers, your DNS servers, or the nodes of an application cluster. If the host you just patched has a problem, only one of them goes down with it.
  • Pin important VMs to specific hosts or groups of hosts. Important VMs to a VCF environment are things like vCenter, VCF Operations, and perhaps your local identity provider and DNS resolver. Create a DRS rule that says they “should” run on a particular host, so that if something does go awry, you can find them without wasting time searching host to host.

Let the Automation Do the Patching

The main way that organizations are surviving the need to update more frequently is through automation. For VCF, vLCM remediates a cluster one host at a time, and you don’t need to sit there and watch it, though you should check in occasionally. If a host fails to remediate, vLCM is designed to stop and report the error. The hosts after it are left as they were. A bad patch does not roll across the whole cluster. If it stops, find out why, fix that, and run it again. A stop usually points at something that makes patching harder than it needs to be.

Shorter host downtime also means less to watch. Live Patch applies eligible ESX patches without restarting the host, and Quick Patch reduces downtime when you patch vCenter. Keep in mind that Live Patch works when you apply patches in sequence. If you skip one, catching up means a traditional restart, which is one more reason to stay current.

Make Patching a Standard Change

ITIL, which originally stood for IT Infrastructure Library, is a widely used framework for running IT services. Many organizations base their change management process on it, even if they don’t call it that. ITIL sorts changes into three types:

  • Standard changes are low risk and follow a defined procedure. They are pre-approved, so they don’t need an individual review each time.
  • Normal changes go through assessment and approval before they are scheduled, often by a change advisory board.
  • Emergency changes need to happen as soon as possible, such as fixing an outage or closing a critical security hole. They get a faster approval process.

Infrastructure patching should be a standard change. Many organizations still treat every update as extremely risky and send every patch through a lengthy change advisory board review. The problem is that the only way to gather enough data to determine if there is truly a risk to your environment is to actually do the update. Without actual data you’re just sitting there letting attackers have a turn.

Patching a host is mostly vMotion and a restart, and even less now with Live Patch. vMotion is probably already a standard change in your organization, whether anyone has explicitly decided that or not. DRS moves workloads with vMotion all day long, and nobody files a change request for it. If moving the workloads off a host is routine, why should patching that host be much different? The risk is lower than it looks, and the way to show that is a track record. Patch in regular maintenance windows, as described below. Use Live Patch and Quick Patch where the patches support them. Keep notes on each patch cycle, such as what you patched, how long it took, and any problems. Bring those notes to the change advisory board. A string of boring patch cycles is the best argument you’ll have.

Lean into the change management definitions, and if your organization doesn’t use the ITIL terms yet, start. A critical vulnerability is exactly what an emergency change is for. Declaring an emergency change for a critical vulnerability is not an abuse of the process, because the risk of not patching is much higher than the risk of patching.

Plan for a Monthly Patching Cycle

When you plan your team’s activities, assume a full patching cycle every month, for everything. Some months will be quieter, and that’s fine, but it’s better to assume the worst. If it takes your team more than a month to patch everything, then work needs to go into finding the slow parts and speeding those up.

Define a weekly maintenance window for management components, such as vCenter and VCF Operations. ESX hosts don’t need one. With vMotion, workloads keep running while a host is patched, and in ITIL terms vMotion is a standard change, or should be.

Consider filing change records in advance, possibly even for the next year or two. You can always cancel them, and it’s worth it to get your maintenance on the schedule so that other activities don’t conflict. If your change managers disagree, get it in writing, and then lean into the emergency changes until they conclude that your planned, monthly approach is way easier to handle. This is doubly true for applications that refuse to vMotion. Those application teams need a specific, planned outage window so they can plan.

In the end, though, none of this makes any single patch go faster by itself. What it does is make patching easier and more routine, and those are the things that make this new reality tolerable in the long term. Slow becomes smooth, smooth becomes fast.

item.content:encoded:
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon returns to North America November 9 to 12, 2026, in Salt Lake City. As organizations bring AI workloads into production, the need to close the gap between experimentation and scalable, secure deployment has never been more urgent. Kubernetes is becoming the common substrate for both AI and modern applications, and the community is moving fast to capture this momentum. That is exactly the conversation we look forward to having at the conference.

Broadcom is excited to return as a Platinum Sponsor, and we look forward to supporting Cloud Native AI + Inference Day on November 9 as a Diamond Sponsor. Building on a rich history as a top contributor to open-source Kubernetes projects, Broadcom continues to be deeply involved in upstream CNCF projects, helping drive innovation, collaboration, and ecosystem growth across the community.

Whether you are a developer, platform engineer, Kubernetes maintainer, or open-source contributor, we would love to chat with you onsite at Booth #129. We are participating in a Cloud Native AI + Inference Day keynote, an executive roundtable, a panel discussion, and several community-led sessions. We have great demos lined up for you, plus plenty of time to connect in person at our booth.

What to Expect at Booth #129

Discover why enterprises choose a unified platform to run VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS), KubeVM Service, and Container Service to deploy AI and all modern applications. Stop by to see how a single, conformant Kubernetes foundation supports all workloads with consistency, privacy, and portability.

  • Open and extensible networking ecosystem with native integration for CNI plug-ins, offering choice and flexibility for partner add-ons
  • Built-in integration with platform engineering tools such as Tekton, Argo CD, Harbor, Headlamp, and Helm, to avoid costly retooling
  • Multi-cluster lifecycle management, policy, and backup for enterprise grade deployment at scale, leveraging OPA Gatekeeper and Velero

Live demos at the booth

Watch our engineers walk through hands-on demos:

  • Configure Kubernetes in minutes – Rapid deployment, on-demand versions, and scalability
  • Deploy workloads in a powerful ecosystem – Conformant Kubernetes with packages and flexible container choices
  • Operate KubeVMs – Deploy VMs through Kubernetes APIs with KubeVM Service
  • Deploy AI workloads securely – Keep your data private and secure, simplify infrastructure, and streamline model deployment

Interactive Platform Experience

Our team will also walk you through the platform capabilities that support these demos and answer any questions you have as you gain first-hand experience with the three core services:

  • A CNCF certified Kubernetes runtime to innovate with the broader ecosystem and run all apps
  • KubeVM Service to deploy and manage VM-based applications using Kubernetes workflows
  • Container Service to deploy single instance containers without using Kubernetes workflows

Booth Theater Sessions

Our experts take the stage to explore the future of open-source innovation, enterprise AI, and cloud-native infrastructure. Across these sessions, you will discover the latest open-source contributions — including KubeVM, Velero 1.19, COSI, and Image Builder — alongside deep dives into VKS 3.8, Kubernetes 1.37, agentic AI workloads, automated chained upgrades, and actionable paths for getting involved in upstream Kubernetes as contributors and maintainers.

Meet our open-source contributors

Meet our experts who are contributing to foundational and popular open source projects such as Velero, Cluster API, etcd, Containerd, Harbor, Contour, and others. Our engineers are available for 1:1 conversations to discuss open source solutions that simplify, secure, and scale applications. You can also discuss VKS, KubeVMs, and Container Service, including upcoming capabilities and roadmap directions, or schedule a deeper dive with our technical experts.

Don’t Miss the Cloud Native AI + Inference Day Keynote

Topic: Path to Resilient App Delivery: AI is Hard, Production is Harder

  • Time: Monday, November 9, 10:10 a.m.
  • Location: Salt Palace, Level 2, Room 254

Executive Roundtable

Join us for an executive roundtable hosted by Broadcom, Canonical, and PlatformEngineering.org.

  • Topic: Scaling Secure and Governed AI Platforms
  • Location: Matteo Ristorante Italiano, Salt Lake City
  • Time: 4 – 6 p.m, Wednesday, November 11
  • Register to secure your spot for this closed door roundtable discussion

Reception and Panel Discussion

Join us for a reception and panel discussion hosted by Broadcom, Canonical, and PlatformEngineering.org.

  • Topic: Building The Agentic Future
  • Location: Matteo Ristorante Italiano, Salt Lake City
  • Time: 6 – 9 p.m, Wednesday, November 11
  • Register to join your peers over food, drinks, and some great conversations

Expo Theater Session

Title : One Kubernetes API for VMs, without rebuilding the infrastructure beneath it 

  • Time: Tuesday, November 10, 2:35 p.m.
  • Location: Demo Theater, Expo Floor

Join this session to discover how VM API, an open-source CNCF Sandbox project, brings Kubernetes’ declarative simplicity to virtual machines through a platform-agnostic VirtualMachine resource and status contract modeled after Cluster API. This session will examine the core architecture and provider interface, demonstrate cross-platform portability across two distinct environments, and show how this unified model enables advanced capabilities like replicas, rolling replacements, and warm pools of pre-provisioned VMs.

Sign up for Expert-led KubeCon Community Breakout Sessions

Dive Deeper into VKS

For those who want to get a head start or dive deeper before the event, we encourage you to explore our blog posts:

  • Deploy Apps Faster, Scale Smarter, and Lower Your TCO with VKS in VCF 9.1
  • VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service 3.7

Join Us in Salt Lake City

Join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in Salt Lake City. Connect with our engineers and maintainers at Booth #129 and be part of the conversations shaping the next decade of cloud native infrastructure.

See you in Salt Lake City.

item.content:encoded:
Overview and Call to Action

While critical advisories are not typical blog topics, protecting customer environments and preventing unexpected data loss is our top priority. We are leveraging every communication channel available to ensure platform and infrastructure administrators are aware of a critical upgrade prerequisite.

If you run vSphere Supervisor or VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) clusters and are planning an upgrade to vCenter Server 9.1.0 or 9.1.1, you must verify the vLCM/VUM database schema prior to initiating the upgrade.

Under specific conditions, upgrading without verifying and remediating database scheme inconsistencies caused by a vLCM/VUM reset will result in Supervisor Control Plane Virtual Machines (VMs) and Foundation Load Balancers (FLBs) being removed and lost.

Environment and Applicability Matrix

Please review the following matrix to determine if your environment requires pre-upgrade verification:

What Causes This Issue?

In earlier releases (vCenter 8.0 Update 3 through 9.0.x), administrators experiencing depot synchronization issues or patch repository corruption may have executed the standard vLCM database reset script documented in Broadcom KB 316581.

While this reset cleared depot corruption, running it on affected 8.0U3 or 9.0.x builds inadvertently caused database schema inconsistencies, specifically dropping required placement policy columns and relation tables.

When upgrading to vCenter 9.1.0 or 9.1.1, the new Lifecycle and Cluster Management (LCCM) subsystem relies on these database relations to discover and manage system VMs. Because of the missing schema definitions, LCCM operations cannot reconcile the Supervisor state, leading to the deletion of Supervisor Control Plane VMs and FLBs from inventory.

What You Need to Do

To ensure a seamless upgrade and prevent disruption to your Kubernetes workloads:

1. Before Upgrading (Pre-Upgrade Check and Remediation)

Do not proceed with an upgrade to vCenter 9.1.0 or 9.1.1 until you have verified your database consistency.

Broadcom has published validation and remediation scripts to check for and fix this schema inconsistency before the upgrade is started.

Refer to Broadcom KB 455737: Checking and Fixing VUMDB inconsistency issues after running vLCM reset script on 8.0U3 to 9.0.x for the official database checker script, remediation script, and detailed execution instructions.

Note: Executing a health inspection using the VCF Diagnostic Tool for vSphere (VDT) will likewise identify this issue, returning a [FAIL] VUM SCHEMA CHECK status notification.

2. If You Have Already Upgraded and Encountered Missing Supervisor VMs

If an upgrade to 9.1.0 or 9.1.1 has already completed and your Supervisor Control Plane VMs are missing from inventory, immediate recovery requires reverting to your pre-upgrade backup/snapshot and restoring the Supervisor state before applying the database fix.

Refer to Broadcom KB 457944: After upgrading to VCF 9.1 or VCF 9.1.1 from either 8.0U3 or 9.0.x, the Supervisor Control Plane VM’s are no longer in inventory for the official recovery workflow.

Official Reference Links

For the latest updates, validation utilities, and authoritative remediation steps, always refer directly to the official Broadcom Knowledge Base articles:

  • Broadcom KB 455737 — Checking and Fixing VUMDB Inconsistency Issues After Running vLCM Reset Script (Authoritative Fix & Checker Scripts)
  • Broadcom KB 457944 — Supervisor Control Plane VMs No Longer in Inventory Post-Upgrade (Issue Overview & Recovery)
  • Broadcom KB 316581 — Reset VMware Lifecycle Manager Depot in vCenter Server Appliance

Summary

Before scheduling or initiating your next upgrade cycle to vCenter 9.1.x:

  1. Verify your environment using the checker script in KB 455737.
  2. Remediate if prompted by the script or VDT.
  3. Back up your vCenter Server and Supervisor prior to performing any upgrade.

If you have questions or need assistance evaluating your environment, please open a support request through the Broadcom Support Portal referencing KB 455737.

item.content:encoded:
(Day 7 of 22 in our Cybersecurity Awareness Month series. Today: certificates)

Certificates generate more questions than almost any other security topic we cover. We find that most of those questions come from misunderstandings about what certificates do. The biggest one is that a certificate means you can trust something. Truth is, it mostly means the connection is encrypted.

A certificate does two things. It helps two computers encrypt what they say to each other, and it’s good at that. It also makes a claim about who is on the other end, and whether that claim is true depends on people a lot more than on technology.

What Certificates Do

Many certificate questions come from not knowing what a certificate is for, so we’ll start there.

How Do You Exchange Keys With Someone You Don’t Know?

To encrypt a conversation, both sides need to share a secret key. That is easy if you can meet first and agree on one. Computers on a network usually can’t.

Public-key cryptography solves this. Each side creates two related keys, a private key and a public key. You keep the private key to yourself, and you can hand the public key to anyone. A message encrypted with your public key can only be decrypted with your private key. Problem solved, as long as the other side can find your public key.

What Is Inside a Certificate

The remaining problem is finding the other side’s public key. That is what a certificate carries. Transport Layer Security (TLS), the protocol that secures network connections, reads the public key from the certificate the server presents.

A certificate also carries the server’s names, the organization, the issue and expiration dates, and the name of the certificate authority (CA) that issued it. The CA adds a digital signature, which lets anyone check that nobody altered the certificate.

Certificates Are Not Trust

The CA’s signature was meant to do more than protect the certificate. It was meant to vouch for the owner. The idea is that you trust the CA, so you can trust what the CA signed.

Encryption Without Trust

In practice it is not that simple. Anyone who controls a domain name can get a certificate within minutes, often at no cost. That has been very good for the internet, because it put encryption on a huge number of web sites.

It also means a certificate says little about who you are dealing with. A personal blog gets a certificate, and so does a small business. But malware sites and ransomware gangs get them, too. All of those connections are encrypted. Whether you should trust what is on the other end is a separate question, and the certificate does not answer it.

A Browser Warning Is an Opinion

Your browser decides whether to warn you by checking the certificate against a list of CAs. That list ships with the browser or the operating system, and it is long. Anyone with administrative access to your computer can add to it.

So when a browser shows no warning, it is saying that the connection is encrypted and that a CA on its list signed the certificate. It is not saying the application is safe. When a browser does show a warning, the connection may still be encrypted properly. Something about the certificate did not match what the browser expected.

A warning is still useful. It can be a hint that something is misconfigured or wrong. Treat it as a hint and find out why it appeared.

This is also one of the main places where security and compliance diverge. A compliance framework may require encrypted network connections. Some organizations read that as “no browser warnings,” and those are different goals.

People Establish Trust

In VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), the people who run the environment establish trust. When you add a host, you are asked to confirm that it is the host you expect, using the SHA-256 fingerprint. When you approve, you are vouching for it. Encryption is automated, but trust is a decision that somebody makes.

It also helps to ask who needs to trust a management interface at all. Only your administrators should be able to reach it. If 100,000 employees need to trust a certificate, you have a hard distribution problem. If ten administrators do, the problem is small. Besides, you should have access controls and firewall rules preventing 100,000 employees from even being able to reach the management interfaces.

How VCF Uses Certificates

VCF encrypts its management connections with TLS, which means it uses a lot of certificates. Every VMware ESX host has one. VMware vCenter has several, and so do the other components. Even though appliance services are behind a reverse proxy, it is still too many to manage by hand, not to mention coordinate timing for replacement. As such, VCF automates it.

The VMware Certificate Authority

The VMware Certificate Authority (VMCA) is built into vCenter. It is just enough of a CA to issue and renew the certificates inside your environment, and it is not a general-purpose CA. Its root certificate is created when you install vCenter, so it is unique to you, even though the name on it says “VMware Engineering” and such (you can change that if you replace the CA root).

This causes friction with public key infrastructure (PKI) teams, because they have a checklist for what a CA does (usually the checklist they, themselves, are judged on). The VMCA has no certificate revocation list (CRL), for example. It doesn’t need one, because people manage the trust. To revoke a host’s certificate, you remove the host.

Four Ways to Run It

  1. Fully automated: This is the default. The VMCA issues and renews everything, and administrators import its root certificate into their own browsers if they want the warnings to stop.
  2. Hybrid: The VMCA still automates the certificates inside the environment. You replace only the certificate that people see when they log in, using one from a CA your browsers already trust.
  3. Intermediate/Subordinate CA: Your enterprise CA signs the VMCA’s certificate, so everything the VMCA issues is trusted wherever your enterprise CA is. This can scale well. PKI teams often object, because the VMCA can then issue certificates in the organization’s name. A good compromise might be a separate CA for infrastructure, apart from the main enterprise one. Administrators keep the automation, and the PKI team keeps the infrastructure certificates apart from the rest of the organization’s.
  4. Fully custom: You turn the automation off and manage every certificate yourself. This is a lot of work; we strongly suggest using the automation instead.

Managing Certificates Across the Fleet

In VCF 9.1, certificate management lives in one place, in VMware Cloud Foundation Operations (VCF Operations). From there you can see the certificates you are responsible for across the fleet, with their expiration dates, their chains, and their renewal status.

You can renew or replace certificates in bulk, and you can sign them with the VMCA inside vCenter, Microsoft Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS), or OpenSSL. Certificates can renew automatically. When you import a certificate, VCF Operations checks that it matches the signing request the component generated, which helps catch a common mistake before it causes an outage.

Some components manage their own internal certificates. VCF Operations raises an alert if one of those fails to renew. There are public APIs for all of this.

Network Encryption Is More Than Certificates

A certificate identifies a server and starts the encryption. The strength of the encryption comes from the TLS version and the cipher suites the two sides agree on.

You do not need to edit individual services to control those. ESX and vCenter use TLS profiles, which set the TLS parameters and ciphers in one place. The default profile is named COMPATIBLE, and ESX 9.0+ added a profile that allows only TLS 1.3. If an auditor asks you to disable older protocols or ciphers, choose a stricter profile. Before you do, check that everything that connects to VCF supports it, including backup and monitoring systems.

The Security Configuration Guide has guidance for configuring TLS profiles. You can find it in our GitHub repository at: https://github.com/vmware/vcf-security-and-compliance-guidelines

What to Do About Certificates

Use the automation. Replacing certificates by hand takes staff time and invites mistakes, both for the VCF admins as well as the PKI admins. The time is often better spent on patching and access control, which usually do more for your security. If it’s a choice between patching systems and changing certificates, patch first.

Only administrators care about management interface certificates. This should be a small group. Limit who can reach the management interfaces. Fewer people then need to trust those certificates, and every certificate decision gets easier.

Talk to your PKI team early. Explain that you want to meet corporate policy with as little manual work as possible, and ask for their help. A dedicated CA root for infrastructure might give administrators the automation and give the PKI team the isolation it wants. Having the PKI team sign the VMCA root certificate, which is the subordinate CA mode described above, is another option. The PKI team gets certificates the organization trusts, and VCF administrators keep the automation. The guide linked in the FAQ below walks through it. By the way, these techniques can help manage certificate complexity in other IT infrastructure systems, too.

Plan for shorter lifetimes. The CA/Browser Forum sets the rules for publicly trusted certificates, and it is shortening how long they can last. The maximum is 200 days as of March 15, 2026, 100 days as of March 15, 2027, and 47 days as of March 15, 2029. Those rules don’t bind a private CA, but expectations tend to follow them. Nobody wants to replace certificates by hand every few weeks.

Watch expirations. Expired certificates take things down, usually at a bad time. Turn on automatic renewal where you can, and use the alerts in VCF Operations for the rest.

Test before you replace. Try a replacement in a test environment first (remember that ESX and vCenter can be deployed as VMs, which makes a great test environment). Take a backup or a snapshot before you change a certificate in production. Broadcom support is excellent, but it’s usually easier to revert a snapshot than to call. Stagger bulk replacements, because each one can trigger components to re-establish trust with each other. Work through VCF Operations which understands these relationships.

Check what connects. After you replace a certificate, confirm that the systems that connect to VCF still work. Backup and monitoring systems are important ones to check right away.

Frequently Asked Questions About Certificates

Q1: My browser says a newly installed vCenter is “not secure.” Is it?

A1: The connection is encrypted. The warning appears because the certificate was created at install time and no CA on your browser’s list signed it. You decide whether to trust it. If you import the VMCA root certificate into your browser, the warning stops.

Q2: Where is the VMCA’s certificate revocation list?

A2: There isn’t one. People manage the trust in VCF, so you revoke a certificate by removing the component from the environment. All a CRL would do here is add complexity, and we like removing complexity.

Q3: Do organizations in regulated industries use the VMCA?

A3: Yes, many do. The automation saves staff time and reduces human error for administrators, PKI staff, and auditors alike.

Q4: Can I use the VMCA to issue certificates for other things, like a web site?

A4: Technically yes, but it is not meant for that. This might be a good place for a short written policy. Agree with your PKI team that infrastructure administrators issue certificates only as part of the built-in automation, for their own management interfaces. They can verify your compliance with their scanners, after all.

Q5: My PKI team does not like intermediate CA/subordinate CA mode. What now?

A5: VCF administrators need some level of automation inside the environment, and a PKI team needs to understand that. Start there, and then offer options. You might ask them to build a separate CA for infrastructure, or build one with them. That can give you the automation and give them the isolation they want.

Q6: Can I use a wildcard certificate?

A6: No. VCF components check the names in a certificate as part of establishing trust, and a wildcard certificate does not name a specific system.

Q7: Can we put a passphrase on the private keys?

A7: No. Services need to start without a person typing a passphrase, or the environment could not recover from a restart unattended.

Q8: My auditor wants older TLS versions and ciphers turned off. How do I do that?

A8: This is a good idea. Use a TLS profile, as described above, and follow the Security Configuration Guide when you configure it. Test it first, because older third-party tools in your environment that connect to VCF may stop working.

Q9: Can I change the organization and location details on the certificates the VMCA issues?

A9: Yes. vCenter has advanced settings, named vpxd.certmgmt.certs.cn.*, that set the country, state, locality, organization, organizational unit, and email address the VMCA puts on certificates. Set them before you renew or replace certificates. Afterward, refresh the CA certificates on your ESX hosts and renew the host certificates, so they pick up the new details. Our guide to subordinate CA mode has the steps:

https://github.com/vmware/vcf-security-and-compliance-guidelines/blob/main/features-capabilities/certificate-management/Configuring-vSphere-Intermediate-Subordinate-CA-Mode.md

Q10: What do you recommend overall?

A10: Don’t make this harder than it needs to be. Spend time on certificates only where it improves security. Administrators, PKI teams, and auditors are on the same team, and each of them worries about things the others have not had to think about. Work it out together.

item.content:encoded:
In Part 1 of this series, we established the backend FinOps architecture within VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF). By combining Custom Groups, custom metadata (Monthly_Budget), Chargeback metering metrics, and policy-scoped Super Metrics, we built an automated alert engine that fires warning notifications the moment a tenant organization breaches 80% of its monthly budget allocation.

However, automated email alerts and event logs are only half the battle. For C-level technology leaders and FinOps steering committees managing dozens of multi-tenant accounts, reacting to individual alert streams is inefficient. True operational excellence requires a centralized, executive-level visualization layer—a single pane of glass that renders tenant spend velocity, visual health colorization, and active guardrail alerts.

This guide walks through the step-by-step creation of the FinOps – Tenant Budget & Spend Governance Dashboard in VCF Operations, specifically updated to address the latest UI layout changes and metric scoping rules.

Step 1: Create the Blank Dashboard Canvas

  1. In VCF Operations 9.1.1, navigate to Operate Dashboards.

2. Click + Create in the left navigation panel under Dashboards.

3. Set the Dashboard Name to: FinOps – Tenant Budget & Spend Governance.

Step 2: Add and Configure Widget 1 – Tenant Budget Health Heatmap

  1. In the bottom Widgets toolbar, locate Heatmap and drag it onto the main canvas.
  2. Hover over the top-right corner of the new Heatmap widget box and click the Pencil icon (Edit Widget).

Section A: Title & Header Settings

  1. Title: Enter Tenant Budget Health Heatmap.
  2. Description: Multi-tenant budget utilization tracking.

Section B: Output Data Accordion Configuration

Expand the Output Data accordion section and set the following parameters:

  1. Configurations: Leave default (Tenant Budget Health Heatmap).
  2. Name *: Tenant Budget Health Heatmap
  3. Group by *: Click the dropdown, expand VCF Automation for All Apps Organization, and select VCFA Organization.
  4. Focus on Groups: Check the box.
  5. Mode: Select the Instance radio button.

Operational Note: Selecting Instance unlocks the specific VCFA Organization object tree. Leaving this on General will prevent the custom budget Super Metrics from appearing in the metric picker.

6. Object Type *: Select VCFA Organization.

7. Attribute type *: Click the dropdown, search for “SM_”, expand Super Metrics, and select: SM_Tenant_Budget_Utilization_Percent (%).

Section C: Color Gradient and Thresholds

    1. Select the checkbox for Solid Coloring.
    2. Set Min Value to 0 (Green).
    3. Set Value to 100 (Red).
    4. Drag or update the middle threshold node to 80 to represent your warning boundary and select Yellow.

Operational Note (Optional): If you want a 4-tier status representation (e.g., Green , Yellow , Orange , Red ), you can click anywhere along the bar to add another node.

5. Click SAVE at the bottom-right corner of the configuration screen.

Step 3: Add the Active Financial Guardrail Alerts Widget (Optional Companion)

To display active budget warning alerts alongside the visual heatmap blocks:

  1. Drag an Alert widget onto the dashboard canvas next to or below the Heatmap.
  2. Click the Pencil icon (Edit Widget) on the Alert widget.

Section A: Widget Header

  1. Set the Title to Active Financial Guardrail Alerts.

Section B: Output Filter Accordion Configuration:

  1. Expand Output Filter Basic.
  2. Scroll through the object types list and select VCFA Organization(#).

Operational Note: In VCFA Organization(#), the number in parentheses indicates your total tenant organization inventory count. In this case, there are now three tenants in the VCFA Organization.

3. Expand Alert Related at the bottom of the Output Filter panel.

4. Click Alert Definitions: Add Alert Definition

5. Search for and select your specific alert rule: Financial Warning: Tenant Budget Threshold at 80%.

6. Drag and drop it to the empty field on the left.

7. Click OK.

8. Click SAVE at the bottom-right corner.

Step 4: Save and Launch the Dashboard

  1. Click SAVE in the top-right corner of the main dashboard builder canvas.
  2. Navigate back to Operate > Dashboards > All and launch FinOps – Tenant Budget & Spend Governance.

Verified Dashboard Behavior and Executive Impact

The completed dashboard completes the end-to-end FinOps lifecycle within VCF Operations.

  • Visual Multi-Tenant Heatmap: Automatically plots wrapped tenant organizations (acme, acme-sales, etc.) as dynamic tiles. Tiles automatically transition across color-coding  (Green, Yellow, Red) based on current burn rate against Monthly_Budget.
  • Alert Consolidation: The companion Alert List widget aggregates all active 80% threshold warning alerts for violating tenant organizations, providing immediate diagnostic details, timestamps, and criticality ratings.
  • Executive Decision Velocity: C-level leaders and FinOps practitioners gain a forward-looking view of private cloud spend—allowing proactive quota adjustments, VM rightsizing, or resource cleanup before monthly budget caps are breached.

Conclusion: Continuous FinOps Governance in Motion

Dashboards in private cloud governance are often relegated to static reporting: artifacts reviewed during monthly cost allocation meetings long after capital has been spent. By contrast, the FinOps Tenant Budget & Spend Governance Dashboard built in VCF Operations operates as an active financial control panel, bridging the gap between infrastructure telemetry and board-level fiscal accountability.

By pairing continuous heat-map visualization with live 80% threshold guardrail alerts, IT leadership and FinOps practitioners achieve three immediate strategic outcomes:

  • Intra-Month Burn-Rate Control: Infrastructure spend is no longer a month-end surprise. Operations teams gain immediate visual feedback as tenant organizations approach their fiscal limits, providing the runway needed to audit unattached storage, clean up orphaned snapshots, or adjust capacity quotas before overruns occur.
  • Policy Standardization Across Multi-Tenant Fleets: Whether governing two tenant accounts or two hundred, the combination of Custom Group metadata containers and policy-scoped Super Metrics enforces uniform, automated financial guardrails across every business unit without adding administrative overhead.
  • Demonstrable Private Cloud ROI: By bringing dynamic fiscal governance to private cloud workloads, technology leaders fulfill the ultimate promise of enterprise FinOps: pairing self-service agility with predictable, margin-protective economic control.

With the backend alert engine active and the executive dashboard online, your VMware Cloud Foundation environment transforms spend governance from a reactive administrative burden into a continuous, system-enforced discipline.
